title: Examination, Diagnosis & Treatment Planning I — Test

mcqs.q: The Latin phrase “Primum non nocere,” central to the dentist's role, means:
opts: Treat the cause, not the symptom
Do unto others as you would have done
mcqs.explain: “Primum non nocere” = “first, do no harm” — the dentist's first duty in maintaining oral health is to avoid causing harm.

mcqs.q: The three sequential pillars that form the foundation of sound dental care are:
opts: Patient assessment → examination & diagnosis → treatment planning
mcqs.explain: Appropriate care is built on patient assessment, then examination & diagnosis, then treatment planning.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the recognised uses of the patient record/file?
mcqs.explain: The record serves medico-legal, insurance, forensic, follow-up, research and referral purposes — not fee-setting.

mcqs.q: The chief complaint should be recorded:
opts: After the clinical examination is complete
By the assisting nurse, not the dentist
mcqs.explain: The chief complaint is recorded in the patient's own words; the whole treatment plan revolves around it, so the patient should be allowed to speak without interruption.

mcqs.q: Before starting operative treatment, a signed document that the patient must complete is the:
opts: Medical-history form with a consent signature
mcqs.explain: The patient must fill a comprehensive medical-history form and sign the consent form before treatment begins.

mcqs.q: A comprehensive medical history allows the clinician to do all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Guarantee that no emergency will ever occur
Prevent complications on the dental chair
mcqs.explain: The history helps alter, contraindicate or postpone treatment and identify referral needs, but it cannot guarantee zero risk of an emergency.

mcqs.q: For a patient allergic to the latex rubber-dam sheet, the correct measure is to:
opts: Use nitrile, neoprene or vinyl gloves and a tissue napkin under the dam
Proceed normally, as latex allergy is not relevant in dentistry
Use extra latex gloves for a tighter seal
Always avoid any rubber dam for every patient
mcqs.explain: Use non-latex (nitrile/neoprene/vinyl) gloves, place plastic gloves under gloves, and put a tissue napkin before the dam to avoid direct latex-tissue contact.

mcqs.q: A patient with haemophilia is significant in operative dentistry mainly because:
opts: Soft-tissue injury (e.g. from a dam) may cause profuse bleeding
Teeth are more prone to caries
mcqs.explain: In a bleeding disorder the patient bleeds profusely with soft-tissue trauma; consult the physician and treat under medical supervision.

mcqs.q: In an asthmatic patient, which is recommended?
opts: Defer treatment until asthma is controlled and keep an inhaler and oxygen accessible
Routinely use a rubber dam and NSAIDs
Give prophylactic antibiotics before every visit
mcqs.explain: Defer until controlled and free of respiratory infection, keep a bronchodilator and oxygen at hand, and avoid NSAIDs and (usually) the rubber dam.

mcqs.q: Regarding a rubber dam and arterial oxygenation in a HEALTHY patient, the evidence indicates the dam:
opts: Does not reduce arterial blood-oxygen levels
Must never be used on any patient
mcqs.explain: Although a dam can alter nasal/oral airflow, it appears not to reduce arterial blood-oxygen levels in a healthy patient (Goodday & Crocker, 2006).

mcqs.q: In a hypertensive patient undergoing operative treatment, you should specifically:
opts: Double the epinephrine dose for better haemostasis
mcqs.explain: Care is needed with adrenaline/epinephrine in hypertension; epinephrine-impregnated retraction cords are avoided because they can cause tachycardia.

mcqs.q: In a diabetic patient, the main operative precaution is to:
opts: Avoid causing lacerations because healing is delayed
mcqs.explain: Diabetics heal more slowly, so avoid soft-tissue lacerations (e.g. with the dam clamp) and take care during treatment.

mcqs.q: A cardiac patient at risk of infective endocarditis can receive dental care provided that:
opts: Prophylactic-antibiotic coverage is given for high-risk procedures
mcqs.explain: Cardiac patients can be treated but with prophylactic-antibiotic coverage to prevent bacterial endocarditis for high-risk procedures (AHA 2007, revised 2019).

mcqs.q: Which dental procedure is classified as HIGH-risk for bacteraemia (needing prophylaxis)?
mcqs.explain: High-risk: extractions, all periodontal procedures, implants, re-implantation and endodontic surgery. Restorative work, dam placement, impressions and fluoride are low-risk.

mcqs.q: Which is a LOW-risk bacteraemia procedure?
mcqs.explain: Low-risk includes restorative dentistry, most local-anaesthetic injections, dam placement, intracanal endodontics, post/build-up, suture removal, impressions, fluoride and radiographs.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised physiologic change with aging relevant to operative dentistry?
opts: Xerostomia with plaque retention and non-carious wear
mcqs.explain: Aging brings xerostomia, loss of taste/smell, mucosal alterations, plaque retention and non-carious lesions (attrition, abrasion, erosion).

mcqs.q: The dental history is valuable because it primarily helps to:
opts: Predict future behaviour and identify problems while minimising extra radiographs
Replace the need for any clinical examination
Determine the shade of a crown
mcqs.explain: It reveals previous experiences, attitudes and specific problems (food impaction, pain, broken restorations) and helps minimise radiation and additional radiographs.

mcqs.q: Universal infection-control precautions taken BEFORE any hands-on examination include:
opts: Sterilised instruments, disinfected surfaces and personal barriers
mcqs.explain: Before examination: sterilise/disinfect instruments, disinfect operatory surfaces and use personal barriers (gloves, mask, eyewear, gown).

mcqs.q: The correct sequence of the clinical examination is:
opts: Extraoral examination first, then intraoral examination
Radiographs first, then any clinical look
mcqs.explain: The examination has two parts — extraoral (face, TMJ, muscles, nodes) first, then a systematic intraoral examination.

mcqs.q: During the EXTRAORAL examination you look for all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Deviation of the mandible on opening
mcqs.explain: Extraoral exam assesses facial symmetry/proportion, swelling, extraoral sinus-tract openings and mandibular deviation; marginal-ridge findings are part of the intraoral restoration exam.

mcqs.q: The correct order within the intraoral examination is:
mcqs.explain: Intraoral exam is systematic: soft tissues (cheeks, vestibule, mucosa, lips, palate, tonsils, tongue, floor), then teeth, then restorations.

mcqs.q: Examination of esthetic appearance evaluates:
opts: Tooth colour, form, display and position, and gingival-margin symmetry
Only the shade of the anterior teeth
mcqs.explain: Esthetic evaluation covers tooth colour, form, display and position relative to the face, plus symmetry of the gingival margins, with a discussion of realistic expectations.

mcqs.q: A “plunger cusp” noted on occlusal examination refers to a cusp that:
opts: Forces food into the interproximal contact
mcqs.explain: Occlusal examination notes wear facets, enamel cracks, mobility, interferences, TMJ clicking/popping and a ‘plunger cusp’ that impacts food into the contact area.

mcqs.q: The recommended charting sequence begins:
opts: From the most posterior tooth in the upper-right quadrant, progressing across
mcqs.explain: Using the FDI system, charting starts at the most posterior tooth in the upper-right quadrant and proceeds systematically.

mcqs.q: During tooth examination, dental floss is particularly useful to identify:
opts: Overhanging restorations, improper proximal contours and open contacts
mcqs.explain: Floss detects overhangs, poor proximal contours and open contacts; cotton rolls keep the field dry and a mirror/light give clear vision.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of non-carious tooth-surface loss with its cause is CORRECT?
opts: Abrasion — wear from an external agent such as hard brushing
mcqs.explain: Attrition = tooth-to-tooth wear; abrasion = external agent (e.g. brushing); erosion = chemical/acid; abfraction = cervical loss from occlusal flexural stress.

mcqs.q: Clinical evaluation of restorations is performed using:
opts: Visual inspection, tactile exploration, floss and radiographs
mcqs.explain: Restorations are assessed in a clean, dry, well-lit field by visual inspection, tactile exploration with an explorer, dental floss and radiographs.

mcqs.q: “Amalgam blues” seen on examination represent:
opts: A bluish discoloration of thin enamel adjacent to amalgam
mcqs.explain: Amalgam blues are the bluish shine of amalgam through thin enamel; other amalgam findings include overhangs, ditching, voids, fractures, poor contours/contacts and recurrent caries.

mcqs.q: The Modified Ryge / USPHS criteria are used to clinically evaluate:
mcqs.explain: The Modified Ryge/USPHS criteria assess composite restorations: colour match, marginal discoloration, secondary caries, anatomic form, marginal integrity, surface texture, gross fracture and post-operative sensitivity.

mcqs.q: Under the Modified USPHS criteria, ‘surface texture’ is assessed by:
mcqs.explain: Surface texture is checked with the explorer; colour match, marginal discoloration and secondary caries are by visual inspection, while form and marginal integrity use both visual inspection and the explorer.

mcqs.q: Magnifying loupes used in operative dentistry are typically:
opts: 2×–2.5× for multiple quadrants and 3×–4× for several/single teeth, ideally with a light
mcqs.explain: Loupes of 2×–2.5× view multiple quadrants and 3×–4× view several or single teeth, ideally with a light; the dental microscope gives higher magnification and a broader field.

mcqs.q: Diagnostic study models (physical or virtual) are used for all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Study models help with occlusal relationships, treatment planning, patient education and (as virtual models) 3D records — not blood pressure.

mcqs.q: Cervical burnout on a radiograph is:
opts: A radiolucent artefact at the cervix that can mimic caries
A deep carious lesion needing extraction
mcqs.explain: Cervical burnout is a radiolucent artefact between crown and root from X-rays passing through the thinner cervical area; it can mimic caries.

mcqs.q: A key feature distinguishing cervical burnout from true proximal caries is that burnout:
opts: Disappears or changes on a periapical film of the same tooth
mcqs.explain: Unlike true caries, the radiolucency of cervical burnout disappears/changes on the periapical film of the same tooth.

mcqs.q: Radiographs are indicated in operative dentistry to detect all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Radiographs reveal caries (including proximal, recurrent/secondary), overhangs, fractures and cervical burnout; allergy status comes from the medical history, not radiographs.

saqs.q: List the uses of the patient record and the four main categories of information it should contain.
saqs.a: USES — medico-legal, medical-insurance claims, forensic investigation, follow-up, research, referral. INFORMATION — personal details; chief complaint in the patient's own words; comprehensive medical history; dental history.

list: Personal details — name, age, sex, occupation, mobile number, address
Chief complaint — recorded in the patient's own words

saqs.q: Why is a comprehensive medical history important? Give at least four reasons.
saqs.a: It lets the clinician alter the treatment modality, prevent medical complications in the chair, contraindicate certain procedures, postpone treatment, and identify conditions needing referral. It flags communicable disease, allergies and medications, and systemic or cardiac disease.

list: Prevent medical complications on the dental chair
Identify conditions needing referral to or advice from a physician before care

Implication
rows: less strenuous procedures, or antibiotic prophylaxis

saqs.q: Summarise the operative precautions for asthmatic, hypertensive, diabetic and cardiac patients.
saqs.a: ASTHMA — defer until controlled and free of URTI; keep inhaler and oxygen accessible; avoid NSAIDs and usually the dam. HYPERTENSION — care with adrenaline; avoid epinephrine retraction cords. DIABETES — avoid lacerations, healing is delayed. CARDIAC — prophylactic antibiotic cover for high-risk procedures.

head: Condition

take care with adrenaline/epinephrine in the local anaesthetic; avoid epinephrine-containing gingival retraction cords — they cause tachycardia
avoid lacerations (e.g. from the dam) — healing is delayed
prophylactic antibiotic cover for high-risk procedures, to prevent bacterial endocarditis (AHA guidance)

saqs.q: Classify dental procedures by their risk of bacteraemia, giving examples of each.
saqs.a: HIGH RISK (need prophylaxis) — all extractions, all periodontal procedures, implants, re-implantation, endodontic surgery. LOW RISK — restorative dentistry, most LA injections, dam placement, intracanal endodontics, post and build-up, suture removal, impressions, fluoride, radiographs, removable prosthodontic or orthodontic appliances.

saqs.q: Describe the sequence and components of the clinical examination in operative dentistry.
saqs.a: After universal precautions, examine EXTRAORALLY then INTRAORALLY. Extraoral — muscles of mastication, TMJs, lymph nodes, vital structures; face for symmetry, swelling, sinus openings, deviation on opening. Intraoral — soft tissues, then esthetics and occlusion, then the teeth, then the restorations.

ans.text: After universal precautions — sterilised instruments, disinfected surfaces, personal barriers — the examination proceeds extraorally first, then intraorally.

saqs.q: How are amalgam and composite restorations evaluated clinically, and what is cervical burnout?
saqs.a: Evaluate in a clean, dry, well-lit field by vision, explorer, floss and radiographs. AMALGAM — amalgam blues, overhangs, ditching, voids, fractures, poor contours, marginal-ridge incompatibility, poor contacts, recurrent caries. COMPOSITE — Modified Ryge/USPHS criteria. CERVICAL BURNOUT — a radiolucent artefact at the cervix from X-rays through thinner tooth; mimics proximal caries but changes on a periapical of the same tooth.
